transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

For weeks I’ve had this nonstop drive to take on more at the hospital, like I can’t slow my mind or body down even when I know it’s too much. It's really starting to catch up with me, and I just feel completely overwhelmed.
During these past weeks of having this nonstop drive, have you found that you need much less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy?

Yes, during those weeks I was getting by on just three or four hours of sleep because my mind was racing with ideas, but I still felt completely wired and unstoppable. Now that I've crashed, though, I sleep in really late but still wake up during the night and feel totally exhausted.
Have you ever experienced periods in the past, before this recent high-energy phase, where you felt very down, depressed, or lost interest in your usual activities for two weeks or more?

No, I haven't really experienced periods of feeling this down or depressed in the past before this recent cycle started. All of these extreme ups and downs only began recently when I started juggling my new job and preparing for my exams.
Is this recent high-energy phase the very first time in your life you've experienced anything like this, or have you had other separate periods of feeling wired and unstoppable in the past?

Yes, this is the very first time I've ever felt like this, as I'm normally known for being really calm and methodical. This entire cycle of feeling extremely wired and then crashing only started about two months ago when I began juggling my first job, night shifts, and studying for my exam.
Since you've crashed, have you also been feeling down, sad, or lost interest in the things you usually enjoy, and how long has this crash lasted?

Yes, since I crashed I've felt this heavy, sinking sadness every day, like there's no point in trying because I already messed up my job and school. This down phase has been dragging on for close to a month now, starting right after I got written up at work.
During that high-energy period when you were working night shifts and studying, were you using any recreational drugs, new medications, or large amounts of stimulants like caffeine or energy drinks?

I was definitely drinking a lot of coffee, sometimes going through entire shifts on just coffee and forgetting to eat because I felt so wired and busy. But I wasn't taking any recreational drugs or any new medications at all.
During that high-energy period, did you make any impulsive decisions, spend unusually large amounts of money, or engage in risky behaviors that you normally wouldn't?

I didn't really spend large amounts of money or do things like that, but my impulsive decisions were all focused on my work. I kept taking on way too many extra shifts, stayed late charting details without authorization, and ignored my supervisor's instructions because I felt like I knew better than everyone else.
How severely is this low mood affecting your daily life—are you still able to manage basic tasks and work, or has it become nearly impossible to function?

It has become incredibly difficult to function, and even basic tasks like showering or getting dressed feel like dragging my body through mud. Because I feel so drained, I've missed several work shifts and classes, fallen behind on my CNA exam prep, and just can't show up reliably anymore.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or felt that life is no longer worth living during this down phase?

I feel so guilty and defeated that it honestly feels like there's no point in trying, and that my parents and coworkers would be much better off if I had never gotten this job. But even though I feel that heavy and useless, I don't have any thoughts of actually harming myself.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a current severe depressive episode lasting nearly a month, characterized by depressed mood, loss of interest, severe fatigue, sleep disturbance, feelings of guilt/worthlessness, and pessimistic views. The severity is indicated by significant functional impairment, where even basic activities of daily living (showering, dressing) are extremely difficult, and she has stopped attending work and classes. This was immediately preceded by a multi-week period of hypomania/mania characterized by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, grandiosity, and increased goal-directed activity. This presentation is consistent with Bipolar Affective Disorder, current episode severe depression without psychotic symptoms.
